title: A Harvest for the Room
premise: Folklorist Edmund Amberdale arrives in the dying village of Hollowmere to record its harvest songs, but every house he enters shows the same anomaly: an extra chair in old photographs, empty and waiting. He learns the founders bound a hungry presence to the village with a ritual that requires a newcomer to complete each cycle, and the villagers have been grooming him as the offering while pretending to welcome him. As Edmund uncovers the truth, he must choose between fleeing and finishing the ritual himself on his own terms. In the end he rewrites the ritual's final verse, binding the presence to the village's collective memory instead of a single body, and stays as Hollowmere's keeper—no longer invisible, but never again one of them.
about_author: H. M. Sandoval is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing oral histories from rural communities that no longer exist on maps. They write horror about the quiet bargains small places make to survive.

chapters.title: The Road That Narrows
chapters.summary: Edmund arrives in Hollowmere by bus, recording field notes on the strange silence of the hedgerows. The villagers are polite but watchful, and innkeeper Mrs. Tarrow gives him a room with a chair he didn't ask for. POV: Edmund. Beat: unease dressed as hospitality.

chapters.title: Songs They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: At the harvest hall, Edmund records a threshing song, but the singer, old Bram, refuses to repeat the final verse and leaves mid-verse. The villagers go quiet when Edmund plays it back—the recording contains a second, lower voice. POV: Edmund. Beat: first crack in the village's facade.

chapters.title: Grandma's House
chapters.summary: Edmund lodges temporarily in a boarded cottage belonging to a deceased local woman, cataloguing her belongings. Among family photographs spanning a century, every image after 1921 includes one extra empty chair. POV: Edmund, with diary fragments of the grandmother. Beat: dread becomes personal.

chapters.title: The Counting of Doors
chapters.summary: Edmund begins compulsively counting doors each night after hearing footsteps that stop just outside his room. Mrs. Tarrow's advice—keep the lights on, count the doors—echoes the grandmother's diary. POV: Edmund. Beat: paranoia takes root.

chapters.title: What the Children Know
chapters.summary: A village girl, Ivy, draws pictures of the extra chair and tells Edmund 'it saves a seat for the helper.' Her parents snatch her away, terrified. POV: Edmund. Beat: the village's complicity surfaces.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: In the church archive, Edmund finds the founders' ledger: a ritual of 'the Room' that binds a presence beneath the village, renewed every generation by an outsider's consent. The last entry is dated one year before his arrival. POV: Edmund. Beat: the stakes become clear.

chapters.title: A Warm Welcome
chapters.summary: The village throws Edmund a feast, honoring him as 'guest of the harvest.' He notices every toast subtly asks for his promise to stay through winter. Bram, drunk, whispers: don't promise anything. POV: Edmund. Beat: warmth with teeth.

chapters.title: The Chair in the Night
chapters.summary: Edmund wakes to find the extra chair from the photographs standing in his room, warm to the touch, facing his bed. The doors he counted are all one fewer than yesterday. POV: Edmund. Beat: the haunting turns intimate.

chapters.title: Bram's Confession
chapters.summary: Bram admits he was the 'helper' fifty years ago, spared when his brother took his place, and has sung the binding verse ever since to keep the Room fed. He is dying; the village needs a replacement. POV: Bram, then Edmund. Beat: guilt as inheritance.

chapters.title: The Village That Stays
chapters.summary: Edmund tries to leave; the road loops him back to Hollowmere no matter which direction he walks. The villagers watch him return with pity, not surprise. POV: Edmund. Beat: entrapment made literal.

chapters.title: Ivy's Warning
chapters.summary: Ivy secretly gives Edmund the grandmother's missing diary pages, which describe a 'second verse' the founders suppressed—a way to bind the Room without a body. The pages are written in a hand that isn't quite the grandmother's. POV: Ivy, then Edmund. Beat: a thread of hope, frayed at the edges.

chapters.title: The Harvest Eve Procession
chapters.summary: The village walks the field boundaries at nightfall, each house leaving a lit lamp and an empty chair on its step. Edmund understands: the whole village is a ritual circle, and he is walking inside it. POV: Edmund. Beat: awe curdling into horror.

chapters.title: What Mrs. Tarrow Keeps Below
chapters.summary: Edmund breaks into the inn's cellar and finds the original ritual chamber beneath Hollowmere: the Room itself, a threshold of packed earth and nineteen chairs, eighteen occupied by something that is no longer bone. POV: Edmund. Beat: the horror made physical.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: The village elders formally ask Edmund to consent: take the nineteenth chair, keep Hollowmere safe for another fifty years, and be remembered forever as its savior. They promise him belonging. POV: Edmund and the elder Maren Hale. Beat: temptation articulated honestly.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: Edmund refuses publicly at the harvest hall. The masks drop: doors lock, lamps gutter, and the villagers' faces show not anger but relief—they tried, and now the Room may take what it wants. POV: Edmund. Beat: betrayal and abandonment.

chapters.title: Nineteen Chairs
chapters.summary: The presence rises through the village, taking the shape of everyone Edmund recorded singing. Bram dies at his threshold, the binding verse failing in his throat. The empty chairs fill one by one across Hollowmere. POV: Edmund, Bram's last hours. Beat: the price of survival comes due.

chapters.title: The Second Verse
chapters.summary: Edmund deciphers the suppressed verse in the grandmother's diary: the Room was never meant to be fed, but witnessed—it hungers to be remembered, not consumed. The founders chose feeding because witnessing required staying forever. POV: Edmund. Beat: revelation reframing the horror.

chapters.title: The Choice of the Chair
chapters.summary: In the chamber below, Edmund sits in the nineteenth chair—not as an offering but as a witness—and begins to sing the harvest song's final verse, the one no villager would sing twice. POV: Edmund. Beat: courage as acceptance, not defiance.

chapters.title: What the Room Wanted
chapters.summary: The presence stops. It is the founders' first harvest, starved of memory, and it recognizes Edmund's recordings—the songs it was sung before it was bound. Edmund offers it his tapes, his notes, his name in the ledger. POV: Edmund and the presence. Beat: climax—compassion against hunger.

chapters.title: The Rewriting
chapters.summary: Edmond completes the ritual as witness and archivist: the Room is bound to the village's collective memory, fed by every song sung, every photograph kept. The extra chair remains in the photographs, but now it is occupied by no one and needed by everyone. POV: Edmund. Beat: resolution through transformation of the bargain.

chapters.title: Keeper of Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Spring comes. The road opens again, but Edmund stays as the village's keeper, teaching children the songs they once refused to sing twice. Ivy asks if he ever thinks of leaving. He counts the doors—nineteen now, all open. POV: Edmund. Beat: belonging earned, not granted.

chapters.title: A Harvest for the Room
chapters.summary: Epilogue: a new folklorist arrives on the bus, and Edmund greets her with a warm room, a lit lamp, and a chair she didn't ask for. He tells her the village's songs, all the verses, and watches her recorder capture a second, lower voice. POV: the newcomer, briefly Edmund. Beat: the cycle continues—changed, but not broken.
